title: Validate inputs against an allowlist at the persistence/trust boundary
rule: Reject any key or enum value not on a known-good allowlist (recursively for nested bodies) inside the write function itself, never via a guessed denylist or compile-time-only TypeScript union; runtime allowlisting is what protects integrity when a future caller passes request-supplied values.
rationale: Recurred in #125/#127 (a denylist of eight content key names let query/transcript and nested {key:...} through) and #154 (addReviewEvent inserted whatever event string it received, with the audit vocabulary enforced only by TS at call sites).

title: An additive merge may only sum genuinely-disjoint deltas; combine re-delivered data idempotently
rule: Before converting a REPLACE upsert into an additive merge, prove each field's per-run value is a DISJOINT delta. Fields sourced from a window re-fetched by updated_at/updated_on (e.g. PRs, and their re-fetched review comments) are re-delivered on every subsequent sync, so additively summing them double-counts permanently. Add only truly-disjoint deltas (e.g. commit committer-date windows); combine re-delivered fields idempotently (max, or recompute from an idempotent source table), and commit-count-weight rate/score fields so a small delta can't drag a large accumulated row toward a plain mean.
rationale: #205: switching git_snapshots to an additive merge fixed commit-drop but would have inflated prs_opened/prs_merged/review_comments_given on every scheduled sync (providers fetch PRs by updated_at, so an active PR is re-fetched and re-aggregated each run). Resolved by max() for PR/review fields and commit-weighted averages for rates.

title: Check and store the same normalized value
rule: A uniqueness/existence guard must be handed the SAME normalized string the write persists. If the guard trims (or lowercases, or canonicalizes) and the write stores the raw value, the identifier that was proved free is not the identifier that was claimed: the stored value resolves nothing forever, and a later honest claim of the normalized form still looks free — so two rows nominally own one identity.
rationale: #255: findIdentityConflict trimmed github/bitbucket/gitlab before findByExternalId, but addDeveloper was handed the untrimmed input. '--github " alice"' passed a lookup for 'alice', stored ' alice', never resolved in buildDevLookupMap, and left 'alice' claimable by a second developer.

title: An idempotent recompute must actually run and retract stale rows
rule: If correctness relies on idempotent recompute, schedule it across the trailing K periods (with a manual recompute path), and have each per-period recompute DELETE rows for entities no longer in the regenerated set in the same transaction; never write a period once and never touch it again.
rationale: Recurred in #123 (created-at attribution was justified by recompute but only the just-completed period ran, losing late-arriving PR activity, and re-attribution left the old developer's rows intact).

title: Keep user-supplied values disjoint from reserved keys and sentinels
rule: Namespace dynamic object keys built from user-controlled names (e.g. prefix t:) so a value can't shadow a structural key, and never overload one string param to mean both a real identifier and a sentinel; thread an explicit discriminated scope instead.
rationale: Recurred in #104 (a team named 'date' overwrote the chart x-axis when written as row[team.name]) and #124 (getTeamPRReviewCoaching used scope:string for both a team name and the 'org' sentinel).

title: Bound and clamp ranges driven by external timestamps
rule: Any loop or window filter whose extent derives from stored/client timestamps must be bounded on both ends: clamp the upper edge to now, cap window length, and never let a single future-dated or skewed row explode the series or inflate counts past a privacy floor.
rationale: Recurred in #106 (buildTrajectory walked week-by-week to max(lastActivity, now), emitting thousands of zero-weeks from one future-dated snapshot) and #132 (loop/nudge aggregates filtered detected_at >= cutoff with no upper bound).

title: A teardown route needs the same in-flight guard as the routes it races
rule: A destructive/teardown route must take the same in-flight overlap guard as the mutating routes it races with. Fire-and-forget runs apply their deferred writes at the END of the run, keyed by something other than the row being deleted and with no re-check that the row still exists — so a delete accepted mid-run is silently undone minutes later by the settling run, restoring exactly the state the teardown removed. Reject with a typed 409 while a run is in flight (or make the deferred writes re-verify their target still exists); note that 'the thing is misbehaving' is the likeliest reason someone reaches a delete endpoint, so the race is the common case, not the exotic one.
rationale: #262: DELETE /api/admin/git/providers/:id purged the container's cursors with no activeSyncs check, unlike POST /:id/sync and /:id/sync-older-history which both guard on it. A sync-now run's cursorAdvances closures write git_last_sync/git_earliest_sync unconditionally when the run settles, so deleting during a long first sync purged the cursors and had them rewritten minutes later.

title: Before deleting state, ask which invariant reads it as proof
rule: Deleting a cursor, watermark, or marker is a data-integrity decision, not hygiene. Before removing one, find every invariant that reads it as PROOF and check whether the proof survives without it. A forward sync cursor is not just 'where this provider got to' — it is the only evidence that the next run's window is disjoint from what is already stored, which is what licenses an additive merge. Forgetting it re-arms a permanent double-count over data the delete deliberately left behind, and data that is keyed by a coarser identity than the thing being deleted (e.g. rows keyed by provider TYPE, not by the provider row) cannot be retracted alongside it. If the retained data cannot be retracted or the merge made idempotent, the state must not be forgotten — say so instead of asserting the merges absorb the overlap.
rationale: #262: provider delete purged git_last_sync/git_earliest_sync so a re-added provider would honor its first-sync window. But mergeDailyAcrossRuns ADDS commits/lines/files on the stated premise that commit windows are disjoint, upsertRawAuthorDaily has no dedup guard, and raw_author_daily is keyed by provider TYPE — so delete + re-add + re-sync would permanently double every commit metric in the re-imported span, and git_snapshots (a pure projection) would propagate it. The issue's out-of-scope note asserted the merges were idempotent; they are idempotent only for the max()-combined PR/review fields.

title: Security gates must fail closed and validate at runtime
rule: An authorization/approval gate must reject any unrecognized value (fail-closed), validate the value with a runtime allowlist rather than a compile-time union, and be inverted so the permissive branch is the only explicitly named one.
rationale: Recurred in #152 (the publish gate used positive equality gate === 'required-approval', so any typo or unvalidated route param fell through and published with no approval check).

title: A self-asserted scope label is not authorization
rule: If a route accepts a team/org scope from the request to bound an action, verify the actor is actually bound to that scope by the role model; otherwise it is just a label and must be documented as such, not treated as verified authority.
rationale: Recurred in #130 (a 'team-bounded lead removal' took team from the body with no actor-team binding, so any admin could remove any team's example).

title: A claim about persisted state must be emitted from the write that makes it true
rule: When a run emits a line whose truth depends on this run's data actually being KEPT — 'nothing re-asks these', 'the understatement is permanent', 'N rows were written' — do not push it where it is formatted. Every fetch/compute function sits upstream of the keep/discard decision and cannot see it, so a line pushed there fires on every discard path too (an incomplete run holding its cursor, a rolled-back write transaction, a container deleted mid-run). Thread it out as a staged array and push it from the ONE place that knows: inside the commit, after the cursor advance, below the same writability guard the data writes take. Split a mixed message at that seam rather than gating the whole thing: facts that are true the moment they happen (requests made, wall time, counts attempted) stay unconditional, and only the persisted-state half is staged. Enumerating the discard paths at the push site is how this gets got wrong — gate on the advance having actually run, which is true on every keep path and false on all of them.
rationale: #280: the new diff-loss advisory copied the 'this run has recorded its window as covered, so nothing re-asks them' sentence from #275's drop advisory but not its staging, so it fired on all three discard paths — claiming permanent loss over a window that was re-fetched intact next run, and pointing the operator at a destructive repair for it. #275 had already been through the identical bug once (its first version missed the deleted-container path).

title: Before adding a retry, ask whether the retried call can succeed PARTIALLY
rule: A retry only makes a failure rarer if the retried call is all-or-nothing. If the call can return NORMALLY after losing some of its members (a per-item fan-out that swallows a per-item fault and returns the survivors), the retry makes partial success the LIKELY outcome of a healing outage — and a normal return clears the incompleteness flag, advances the cursor, and turns what used to be a loud, self-healing total failure into a permanent silent gap. Worse, the heal is then reported as a recovery over lossy data. Before wrapping a call in a retry, enumerate its internal catch blocks: every one that swallows and continues must either propagate (so the fault reaches the retry and then the cursor hold) or be proven non-lossy. Check sibling adapters for the same fault class — the one that swallows where the others re-throw is where the loss lives, and asymmetry across a provider family is the tell.
rationale: #272: github.ts swallowed EVERY per-commit detail error while bitbucket/gitlab re-throw anything that is not a typed 404. On GitHub the detail response IS the commit, so a swallowed failure dropped it, getCommits returned normally, commitsComplete stayed true and the cursor advanced past the gap. Pre-retry a total outage threw and held the cursor (no loss); the new in-run repo retry made PARTIAL success probable and stamped 'Recovered after retry' on the result.

title: Never memoize a value derived from a response you have just judged unusable
rule: A memo/cache with no invalidation path freezes whatever it is handed as the permanent answer, so a value read off a response the code has ALREADY decided is malformed must never be written to it. And do not stop at the memo: guarding only the cache while still writing the same fabricated value into the append-only row protects the cheap, re-fetchable side and leaves the expensive side corrupt. When one field of a response is unusable, ask which OTHER fields were read from that same body — they are equally suspect. Prefer routing the whole body to the recoverable channel (throw, so a retry and then the cursor hold can act) over salvaging part of it and inventing zeros for the rest, because an empty array is often documented downstream as an ANSWER and will suppress the fallback that would have re-fetched it.
rationale: #275: a list-row fallback recovered a commit whose detail body had no usable `commit` object, but read additions/deletions/diffs off that same body — so the commit landed in raw_author_daily (additive, append-only, cursor advanced) with 0 churn, and `diffs: []` suppressed the sync loop's getCommitDiff fallback because `[]` is documented as an answer. Guarding only the commit_diffstats `put` (which has no invalidation) fixed the re-fetchable half and left the permanent half.

title: Reuse the canonical helper instead of cloning shared logic
rule: Before hand-rolling SQL/math, a gate check, a row decoder, preference plumbing, a duplicate column, or visibility resolution, find the existing canonical helper and reuse or extract it; a second copy (or a hardcoded flag literal, or a duplicate stored value) creates a second source of truth that silently drifts.
rationale: Recurred in #104 (re-derived tier/trend SQL), #107 (re-implemented override gate by hardcoding the flag), #122/#126/#130/#131 (byte-for-byte copied period-walk/decode/coerce/preference plumbing), #123 (rework_rate duplicate column), and #155 (re-implemented visibility orchestration and forked a quieter row decoder).

title: Docs, config keys, and parity claims must match the code
rule: Verify every documented config key against the actual loader (loaders silently ignore unknown keys), and never justify a change by claiming it 'mirrors' another module unless that module actually does the same thing; note deliberately out-of-scope alignments.
rationale: Recurred in #108 (docs said dashboard_base_url but the key is dashboard_url, yielding Slack alerts with no deep link and no error) and #145 (docstrings claimed parity with Pillar 3 cohort resolution, which actually filters by per-developer opt-in, not team-level exclusion).

title: Test every failure path, mode, edge, and budget that can actually trip
rule: Size perf assertions to a realistic org, cover documented edges/boundaries and >=2-item degenerate cases (not just the single-item happy path), exercise both branches of dual-mode components and every exposed query filter, add a failing-hook rollback test for each distinct transaction shape, and assert server DTO mapping by seeding real data and reading it back through the API rather than a frontend fixture.
rationale: Recurred in #108/#105/#106 (the <2s perf test ran on ~5 developers and edge/boundary cases had zero coverage), #152 (rollback was tested only for publish() not the submit() auto-publish path), #162 (the DTO test asserted only four fields), and #163 (the editor's edit path and the browse 'team' filter were untested).

title: Don't build scope without a real production caller
rule: Build exactly what the issue's acceptance criteria require: do not add config knobs, precedence chains, alternate code paths, network transports, scoring algorithms, runtime predicates/guards, or layered wrapper functions whose only callers are tests or their own definitions; defer the seam until a real consumer exists.
rationale: Recurred in #102 (speculative per-team overrides and percentageBaseline mode), #125/#127 (uncalled RealtimeCoach config and httpCaptureTransport), #154 (a 3-line rule fractured into uncalled wrappers and read helpers), #157 (90 LOC of a sibling task's scoring), #159 (test-only options object), and #162 (test-only SCOLDING_WORDS blocklist/isEncouraging predicate).

title: Assertions must be able to fail against the real leak vector
rule: Every negative/privacy assertion must match a string or shape the code actually emits, with a seeded positive control that produces the signal; decode BLOB columns to strings before scanning for forbidden plaintext (JSON.stringify serializes Buffers as integer arrays), and drive sanitizers/security controls through the real execution path (e.g. the actual MATCH query), not just their returned string.
rationale: Recurred in #133 (assertions checked capital-Y 'You were active', an id substring with no carrying field, and BLOB markers invisible because Buffers serialized to integer arrays), #155 (FTS-injection safety was asserted only on the builder's returned string), and #162 (the test relied on a hand-built frontend fixture that cannot catch a server mapping error).

title: A completion signal is not a currency claim
rule: When a cap, chunk, or bound makes 'the run completed' stop implying 'the data is current', the operator surfaces must distinguish the two and report the new in-between state — the run that succeeds while the data is still months old is exactly the one an operator reads as an all-clear. Never infer a positive health claim from narrower checks returning empty: state only what was measured, or add a positive check for the claim you want to make. Partition exclusions must key on the underlying state, not on a display threshold — a condition held below its reporting threshold still falsifies the opposite claim.
rationale: #235: a catch-up cap created 'complete run, cursor still 170 days back'. Right after excluding the repo that caused a stall, the streak cleared and doctor printed 'All N provider(s) advancing' while ~170 days of snapshots were still missing. The added lag signal then keyed its stall-exclusion on the >=3 REPORTING threshold, so a provider held 1-2 runs was printed as 'catching up - advancing' while its cursor was in fact held; and the all-clear was inferred from both readers being empty, which is not evidence of currency.

title: Validate entity existence and lifecycle state before a write
rule: Before writing a flag, endorsing/ranking, or appending an audit/outcome row, fetch the target and assert it exists and is in the expected lifecycle/precondition state (returning a typed not_found/not_published error, not a raw DB error), and require FK or existence/canonicalization checks on actor and functional-key columns; a non-blank check alone lets a typo/ghost id write a row that silently does nothing.
rationale: Recurred in #157 (endorsePractice/orderPracticePool acted on draft/removed rows and surfaced a raw SQLITE_CONSTRAINT), #126 (recovery/complete logged unconditionally without a matching open initiate), and #151/#154 (audit actor/author ids had no FK and a mis-cased team recorded a hide that hid nothing yet 'succeeded').

title: Wrap read-modify-write and multi-statement writes in a transaction
rule: Any read-then-write that preserves omitted fields, or any check-then-act/multi-statement mutation (including MAX(version)+1), must run inside a single db.transaction; a UNIQUE backstop turns a race into a fail-fast error, it does not serialize.
rationale: Recurred in #156 (setPracticeDetails did a non-atomic read-merge-UPSERT) and #151 (addContributionVersion computed MAX(version)+1 in a deferred tx with a doc overstating collision safety).

title: Make ordering correct, total, and deterministic
rule: Order semantic enums by an explicit numeric rank (CASE/rank map) not lexically; make comparators total (never NaN, sort missing rows to a stable extreme rather than coalescing to a real value); and break ties on a monotonic insertion key (rowid), never a random UUID.
rationale: Recurred in #102 (ORDER BY severity DESC on a text column sorted lexically, burying the highest severity last), #105 (metrics coalesced to NEGATIVE_INFINITY made two no-data rows compare as NaN), and #160 (a same-millisecond pin tiebreak on a random UUID resolved nondeterministically).

title: A guard/loop regression test must reproduce the exact failing condition
rule: A test that guards against an infinite render-loop, a reset-on-identity, or any conditional-firing guard must construct the EXACT unstable input the production bug needs — for a fresh-reference-each-render loop, build the array inside the render callback (renderHook(() => hook([], n))), not as a stable renderHook prop. If the test passes with the guard removed, it proves nothing; verify it fails for the right reason (renderHook throws 'Too many re-renders') before trusting it.
rationale: #219: the empty-array 'no reset loop' test passed a stable prop reference per rerender, so it converged with OR without the guard — the guard (sole justification for deleting the stable-empty constants) was effectively untested until the test was rebuilt to create a fresh [] each render.

title: A scoped/single-source write into a multi-source-aggregated row must merge, not replace
rule: When a row aggregates contributions from multiple sources under one key (e.g. git_snapshots keyed (developer, day) merging all providers), any write that runs over a SUBSET of sources must additively merge against the stored row; a full-column REPLACE upsert from a scoped run silently drops the other sources' same-day contribution. Prefer merge-on-conflict, or document the caveat and forbid the scoped path in multi-source deployments.
rationale: #192: per-provider Sync-now (and CLI sync git --provider) ran runSync over one provider and the ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE SET ... = excluded.* rewrote the merged multi-provider day-row from just that provider's data; incremental cursors meant the loss persisted until a state reset.

title: A timestamp compared as a string must be shape-pinned, and its bounds must be total
rule: If a stored timestamp is ever compared with string operators (>=, ORDER BY) rather than parsed instants, pin its shape at the trust boundary with an anchored regex — a toISOString() round-trip is NOT enough, because ISO 8601 expanded/negative years ('+010000-01-01T00:00:00.000Z') round-trip cleanly yet sort before ordinary years and invert every comparison. Make each bound total: compare parsed instants, and reject an unparseable operand explicitly instead of letting NaN compare false and fall through the guard. Where a tighter bound is already provable from state the function has loaded (e.g. a floor can never exceed the forward cursor), prefer it over a looser one like 'before now'.
rationale: #233: the declared history floor is compared lexically against the stored watermark by the backfill's overlap guard, but the validator accepted any value that round-tripped through toISOString(). '+010000-01-01T00:00:00.000Z' passed, and since '+' (0x2B) sorts below '2' (0x32) it read as 'in the past', slipped the upper bound, and bricked the provider's backfill permanently. The same guard also let an unparseable `now` pass, because NaN >= NaN is false.

title: Keep the client/server wire contract in sync
rule: Type a wire field with the same breadth the source guarantees (narrow an unconstrained TEXT column with a safe default rather than asserting a closed union the data doesn't enforce), and when a response shape changes, update every consumer to narrow on the new field before dereferencing, plus its test mock.
rationale: Recurred in #105 (an unconstrained TEXT ai_maturity_basis was cast to a closed union on the frontend) and #131 (the backend wrapped pr-coaching in {enabled,...} but the client still dereferenced data.all_pr and the stale mock masked the TypeError).

title: Label and propagate the true data-quality basis
rule: The data-quality/basis tag must reflect each value's true origin: don't stamp one fixed basis on a metric reading different-tier sources across scopes, don't conflate incomparable quantities under one label, and thread the weakest contributing tier into any derived comparison rather than discarding provenance.
rationale: Recurred in #102 (developer cost mapped to an API estimate and team cost to expense data, both persisted as basis:'git_estimate') and #159 (analyzeUsageSignal compared raw before/after numbers and discarded PeriodMetrics.data_quality).

title: Resolve at the same grain the decision is actually made at
rule: When a derived view answers a question that the write/projection path decides PER ROW (is this attributed? does this resolve?), it must resolve at that same grain. Do not roll rows up to one identity first (MAX/GROUP BY over a mutable column) and resolve the collapsed value: if the rollup picks the resolving variant the unresolved rows are silently hidden, and if it picks the non-resolving one the count includes rows already accounted for elsewhere. Group by the full identity tuple, resolve each variant, then fold only the ones that matter.
rationale: #254: listAuthorCandidates resolved distinctRawAuthors' MAX(author_email) rollup, but the projection resolves each raw row's own (login, email) and sync stamps one run's sample commit email onto every date row that run writes. An author committing from two addresses was therefore either dropped from the review queue while half their history projected to nobody, or listed with a commit_count including already-attributed commits (which auto-create would turn into a duplicate developer).

title: A client gate for a server-authoritative condition must key off the same signal the server enforces
rule: When the UI shows/hides or enables a control based on a condition the server actually enforces (e.g. 'first sync pending' = no stored pipeline cursor), derive the client's decision from the SAME authoritative signal the server checks, not a different, loosely-correlated column. Expose that signal on the DTO (a boolean derived from the real source, resolved in one query, not per-row). A proxy column written by only one code path (e.g. last_sync_at, written only by the sync-now route) goes stale when another path (scheduler/CLI) satisfies the real condition, so the control renders but is silently ignored.
rationale: #228: the window input was gated on last_sync_at while the server gated on the sync_state cursor; after a scheduled/CLI first sync the cursor existed but last_sync_at was null, so the UI offered a history-window that the pipeline discarded.

title: A destructive migration must signal on EVERY path that destroys something, and its predicate must survive the migrations running beside it
rule: A pure-SQL migration cannot print, so its only durable operator signal is a state row a health check reads. Two things then have to hold. (1) The signal must be raised by EVERY destructive path in the file, not just the one whose consequence the author was thinking about — enumerate the DELETEs, and prefer merging paths that destroy the same class of thing into ONE statement so a single `changes()`-gated signal provably covers them all. (2) The predicate must not be built only from tables a SIBLING migration in the same `runMigrations` pass also empties: on the upgrade path with the most to lose, those are already empty by the time the probe runs, so it reports 'nothing to rebuild'. Probe state the neighbours do not touch.
rationale: #266: migration 043's notice probed the four tables migration 042 (running immediately before, in the same pass, with no marker of its own) also empties — so the pre-042 upgrade got a green doctor over stale rollups. Separately, the fail-closed provider DELETE raised the notice while the dedupe DELETE three statements later did not, so a connection's unrecoverable token and its repo-scope filter vanished with no signal on any surface, in exactly the duplicate-container state the migration existed for.

title: A live region announces on a DOM change, not on a state change
rule: When assistive tech must hear an event that can REPEAT with the same wording, do not deliver it by writing the text into state: React bails out of a setState to an Object.is-equal value, so the text node is never mutated and a live region that does not mutate announces nothing. The latch may reason in event identities, but the DELIVERY must be identity-carrying too — put a per-announcement sequence on the KEY of the element holding the text so identical text arrives as a node replacement, in one commit. Reject the two tempting alternatives: clear-then-set across two commits only works if React commits the empty render before the refill lands, which is an assumption about scheduler ordering the code does not enforce, and a trailing-whitespace toggle can be read as unchanged by AT that normalizes whitespace before diffing. The test must assert the DOM mutation (MutationObserver), because a text assertion is satisfied vacuously by the previous announcement's leftover text.
rationale: #278: the sync announcement was latched per RUN but delivered per TEXT, so a retry against the same bad token produced a byte-identical 'Sync failed' and the second failure was announced to nobody — the everyday case, and the fast-settle path where no stage text intervenes to break the tie.

title: A never-throw contract must wrap the operation, not just its arguments
rule: When a component is documented as unable to fail its caller — because the caller's error path is catastrophic — enforce that by wrapping the actual I/O call and EVERY entry point, including construction, not by validating arguments. Argument checks leave the whole infrastructure class (lock contention against a second connection, a full disk, a schema the process did not expect, a constraint a future column adds) escaping into exactly the handler the contract exists to protect. Watch for the eagerly-prepared statement or the constructor-time probe: it sits outside every guard the methods carefully installed, and its throw is usually reported as a caller misconfiguration rather than as the infrastructure fault it is.
rationale: #273: the diffstat cache's docstring said 'a cache write must never be able to fail a sync' and then only range-checked its arguments — so a SQLITE_BUSY from a concurrent CLI run would escape the provider's per-commit loop and, via #231, discard a multi-hour sync. Adding a try/catch fixed the two methods and left the constructor's db.prepare unguarded, where a throw was surfaced as '[type] Skipped — this provider could not be used'.

title: A pinned range bound must derive its hazard from BOTH bounds and the cursor that joins adjacent windows
rule: When a test pins the inclusivity of a window bound, do not reason about the loss direction from that one bound. Check the OTHER bound's inclusivity and how consecutive windows are joined: if a cursor advances to exactly this window's edge so the next window's opposite bound is the same instant, then closed+closed means adjacent windows OVERLAP by one instant, and making the upper bound exclusive is what renders them disjoint. Getting that backwards writes a justification asserting the opposite hazard — and in a codebase whose additive merge is licensed by window disjointness, a comment claiming exclusivity would 'leave a hole' actively defends a permanent double-count. State which direction the pin records and why the current bounds are retained.
rationale: #276: a boundary-row test comment claimed tightening `until` to `<` would leave a permanent hole between backfill chunks. In fact the lower bound is inclusive too (the break is `commitDate < sinceDate`) and a capped run advances the cursor to exactly its `until`, so adjacent windows share that instant — the real exposure is a one-instant double-count through mergeDailyAcrossRuns, which adds commit metrics on a stated premise of disjointness.

title: A prescribed remedy must cover the damage the signal describes
rule: When an operator-facing message names a command as the fix, verify what that command actually rebuilds before naming it — and name its limits. A remedy narrower than the damage IS the false all-clear the signal exists to prevent: the operator follows it exactly, acknowledges, and the residue is left with no signal remaining. Check the range the command defaults to and whether the recovery path you recommend elsewhere narrows it. If a sibling doc already carries the caveat, carry it forward rather than restating the command without it.
rationale: #266: the reset notice prescribed `toprope aggregate backfill --from <the earliest day the resync imported>` while the same migration recommended a controlled resync with a NARROW months window — so every period outside that window kept its pre-reset totals. `backfill` also does not touch `pr_review_metrics` or `coaching_signals` at all. Migration 042 had stated both caveats; 043 reproduced 042's command and dropped its warning.

title: A re-check that guards against 'the thing I was predicated on went away' must compare its IDENTITY
rule: When a long-running operation re-verifies at its write boundary that the entity it started on still exists, compare the OWNER'S IDENTITY (row id), not mere existence. A boolean 'is this key still owned?' cannot distinguish 'the row I was predicated on is still here' from 'a DIFFERENT, newly-created row now occupies that key' — and delete-then-recreate is often the flow the product's own UX prescribes (e.g. when an attribution key is immutable, the remedy IS delete + re-add). Snapshot the owner id before the work starts and require the same id at write time; entities whose ownership cannot change during the operation (config-file-declared, undeletable) should be excluded from the snapshot rather than given a synthetic owner to compare against itself.
rationale: #264: the mid-run ownership gate first asked 'does any git_providers row own this (type, container)?'. An admin deleting a provider and immediately re-adding the same container — exactly what the immutable-container UI tells them to do — left a new row on the pair, so the settling run wrote its pre-delete window under the new provider AND resurrected the forward cursor, making the re-added provider's first-sync window silently ignored: the #262 state the whole issue existed to make unreachable.

title: A recorded consent/authorization value must govern the effect it names
rule: When a route records a consent/authorization value that another surface must honor (e.g. the reach a developer consents to publish at), make the recorded value actually govern the effect, or reject a value that disagrees with the effective governor; a stored-but-never-read consent field is a false guarantee that can silently permit a broader effect than was consented to.
rationale: #189: the approve route collected visibility_scope as 'the reach the developer consents to' and stored it in showcase_consent, but nothing read it back — browse resolves visibility from the draft-time contribution scope, so consenting to 'team' on an 'org' draft still published org-wide. Fixed by binding visibility_scope to equal contribution.scope.

title: A remedy printed to an operator is executable advice — verify it is reachable and safe
rule: Before an error/advisory string tells an operator HOW to fix something, verify the instruction against the code three ways. (1) Is it SAFE? Trace it through the invariants — an instruction the codebase documents elsewhere as corrupting (purging a sync cursor over retained additive rows, re-importing a non-disjoint window) is worse than saying nothing, because the operator trusts it more than their own judgement. (2) Is it REACHABLE for every provenance the message can be emitted under? A route that 409s config-file entities, or a cascade that short-circuits while another owner still resolves, makes the named repair a no-op that looks like a fix. Say so explicitly rather than naming a remedy that half the deployments cannot run. (3) Is it COMPLETE? If the repair resets state to a bounded default (a first-sync window, a retention floor), the recovery step for everything outside that bound is part of the remedy, not an optional extra.
rationale: #280: the advisory told the operator to reset the provider's cursors and re-import — the exact operation the #262 rule documents as re-arming a permanent double-count, and a far larger corruption than the understatement being repaired. The corrected remedy then had two more holes: the admin delete route refuses config-file providers outright and the cascade is skipped while the YAML entry owns the container, and re-adding restores only the 6-month first-sync window, silently dropping older history.

title: A rule re-derived in SQL must be provably equivalent to the code's, and fail closed where it is not
rule: A migration that re-implements a code-side rule in SQL is a SECOND definition, and the two will differ: SQLite's `lower()` is ASCII-only where JS `toLowerCase()` is Unicode-aware, and bare `trim(X)` strips ASCII spaces only where `String.prototype.trim` strips every Unicode Zs plus U+2028/2029/FEFF. State the domain on which they are PROVABLY identical (e.g. ASCII-only input), restrict the in-place rewrite to that domain, and fail closed — delete, refuse, or report — outside it, rather than writing a value the code can never produce. Pin the equivalence with a test that runs the same spellings through both, and pin the SQL expression to every occurrence in the migration file, because SQL gives you no way to name it once. Verify each claim empirically rather than reasoning about it: `trim(X,Y)` is character-wise not byte-wise, `changes()` resets to 0 after a zero-row statement, and JS `.trim()` DOES strip U+00A0/U+FEFF.
rationale: #266: migration 043 first used a 6-character ASCII trim set and claimed the divergence with `normalizeContainer` was theoretical. It was not: a container the migration could not re-spell would be written back as a value no write path can produce, so the delete cascade keyed on it would retract nothing and report success — a permanent ghost. Two review cycles were spent on this, including a comment that was itself factually wrong about which characters JS trims.

title: A safety-guard input must be required and carry the evidence, not a verdict
rule: A parameter that feeds a safety guard must be REQUIRED, never defaulted — an omitted claimant/exclusion list defaults to the permissive answer ('nothing claims this'), so a future caller that forgets it silently destroys shared state. Prefer taking the EVIDENCE (the resolved set the decision is derived from) over a precomputed boolean verdict, so the decision is derived in one place and the value cannot be constructed without it. And fail closed on any member of that set that does not resolve: a loosely-validated config entry whose key resolves to undefined can never match the target, so treat its presence as a claim rather than letting it drop silently out of the set.
rationale: #262: deleteProviderAndSyncState defaulted configProviders to [], the permissive answer to the very question it exists to ask — in the same diff that removed a hardcoded fail-open default from dbProviderToDto for the same reason. dbProviderToDto was then changed to take the cursor SET and derive first_sync_pending itself, collapsing three duplicated derivations into one; and a malformed config entry (providerContainer -> undefined) was made a fail-closed claimant instead of silently unprotecting rows a live config provider still advances.

title: A shared counter must be scoped to the bound it enforces and the value it reports
rule: When one accumulator both enforces a documented ceiling and feeds an operator-facing message, check its scope against BOTH claims. (1) Enforcement: a ceiling named 'per run' must be owned by the run, not declared inside a function the run calls in a loop — otherwise the real ceiling is `bound x iterations`, and any outer retry wrapper multiplies it again. Walk every enclosing loop before trusting the number in the docstring. (2) Reporting: a message scoped to ONE operation must interpolate that operation's own value, not the shared total, or every operation after the first over-reports and sends an operator hunting for an event that never happened. Track a per-call value alongside the shared one. Run length is not a cosmetic concern when a scheduler fires without an in-flight guard: a long run overlaps the next one, and two concurrent runs reading the same cursor into an additive merge are a permanent double-count.
rationale: #272: GIT_RUN_RETRY_SLEEP_BUDGET_MS was declared inside fetchProviderData, which runSync calls per provider, so the documented 40-minute run ceiling was really 40 min x providers — doubled again by runConnectorWithRetry. The same counter was interpolated into a per-fetch heal advisory, so the second repo to heal claimed the whole run's sleep as its own wait.

title: A wiring or placement decision needs a test that fails when it is undone
rule: When the POINT of a change is where something happens — which seam injects a dependency, or which side of a transaction a write lands on — the outcome assertions cannot see it, so name the undo and build the test that fails on it. Two shapes recur. First, if every test mocks the factory/DI seam that installs the component, deleting the wiring leaves the whole suite green while the feature is simply off in production; stop mocking that seam. Second, if the placement is 'outside the transaction', a test that fails BEFORE the transaction proves nothing — the transaction still commits — so force an actual rollback and assert the artifact survived it.
rationale: #273: the provider factory was the only place the cache was handed to a provider and was mocked in every test, so dropping the argument would have silently disabled the ratchet; and the out-of-transaction write, which the issue calls the feature, was only covered by a fetch-time failure, under which the write transaction still commits.

title: A writer must store only what its own reader will accept
rule: When a persistence layer validates on READ — because the column is unconstrained TEXT, or because the DB's type affinity lets a wrong-typed value through — the WRITE boundary must apply the SAME predicate, from one shared definition. A reader stricter than its writer is self-perpetuating and silent: the row is written on every run and rejected on every next one, so a cache never ratchets, a projection never converges, and nothing anywhere reports it. Enumerate what the real producers can emit before assuming the mismatch is unreachable — a field mapped as `a ?? b ?? ''` or `a || b` yields a blank or an undefined that JSON.stringify drops entirely.
rationale: #273: decodeEntries rejected an entry whose path was blank, but Bitbucket maps a diffstat entry with neither `new` nor `old` to path:'' and GitLab to undefined; and decodeRow rejected a fractional total that CHECK (additions >= 0) admits via INTEGER affinity, while GitHub's totals come straight from unvalidated detail.stats. Either would have made the ratchet a permanent no-op for those commits.

title: Advance a re-fetch cursor atomically with, and conditional on, the data it gates
rule: A progress cursor/watermark that controls what a later run re-fetches must be written inside the SAME db.transaction as the data it certifies — never eagerly/auto-committed before or separately from that write — so a failed write rolls the cursor back and the window re-covers next run. When the re-fetched data is combined ADDITIVELY (non-idempotent, e.g. summed commit deltas), an incomplete fetch must be all-or-nothing: persist no rows for that source AND hold its cursor, because writing the partial window now and re-fetching it next run would double-count. Never swallow the write failure into a 'success' result; surface it and report zero writes.
rationale: #231: setProviderLastSyncTime auto-committed per-provider before the snapshot insertMany transaction and a write failure was caught into an error string that still returned success, so a write-tx failure or a single repo's getCommits throw advanced the cursor past a window whose additive commit data was never persisted — a silent, permanent git_snapshots gap that never re-fetched and could not be safely reset.

title: An error branch that unmounts a subtree destroys the state that subtree was proving
rule: Before rendering an error state INSTEAD of a list, ask what per-row state unmounts with it. A data library keeps `data` when a BACKGROUND refetch fails while still flipping isError, so on a polled surface one transient blip swaps the whole list for an error line and takes every row's mount-scoped state with it — refs latching an in-flight operation, mutation results holding a job handle, pending timers. The operation then settles into a remounted row that has never heard of it. Gate the destructive branch on there being nothing to show (`isError && !hasData`) and report a refresh failure ABOVE the retained rows. The corollary for the state itself: if losing it is silent, say in the code that its lifetime is the row's mount.
rationale: #278: `providers.isError ? <error> : <Table>` was checked before hasProviders, so one failed 1s poll during a multi-hour sync unmounted every ProviderRow and lost the announcement latch and the 202 handles — exactly the restart scenario the freshness gate was written to survive.

title: An identity column that resolves attribution must be append-only, not latest-wins
rule: If a stored identity field participates in resolving a row to an owner, do not overwrite it with each run's newest observation. Sampling one value per run and stamping it across rows means the column holds whichever observation landed last, so a row that resolved to an owner can silently stop resolving — and where the derived table also RETRACTS, the next rebuild deletes history that was already correctly attributed. Prefer capturing every observed variant (finer key or an append-only identity table); at minimum make the field first-write-wins so a non-blank value is never replaced by a different non-blank value, and say so where the docstring claims the field 'only ever gains information'.
rationale: #250: upsertRawAuthorDaily merged author_email with bestKnown(), which returns the incoming value whenever non-blank, while sync stamps ONE sampled commit email per (login, run) across every date row that run writes. A developer registered by one of an author's two addresses could have their already-attributed cells deleted by the next whole-day rebuild after a run happened to sample the other address.

title: Bound every factor of a superlinear cost, not just the convenient one
rule: When a guard caps one input to a cost that is superlinear in two or more factors, cap the others too or the guard does not bound anything. A glob/regex denylist compiled from operator config and matched against provider-supplied strings backtracks in O(n^k) on a NON-matching subject — k wildcards, n subject length. Capping k at a plausible-config number (10) while the subject stays unbounded still hangs, and the hang lands wherever the match runs: inside a write transaction, holding the DB lock. Set the cap from what makes the class unreachable, clamp the subject at its own boundary, and document that raising either requires revisiting the other.
rationale: #256: AUTO_CREATE_EXCLUDE_MAX_WILDCARDS was set to 10 with a comment reasoning correctly about ReDoS, but `^.*a.*b...$` against an attacker-chosen author_email (committer-set, unbounded) is O(n^10) and runs inside the sync write transaction. Fixed by dropping the cap to 2 and clamping the matched subject to 320 chars.

title: Bound discovery/list endpoints with an enforced limit
rule: Every list/discovery endpoint must accept and enforce a validated limit (cap plus a 400 on overflow) and plumb it into the query; do not return the entire visible set.
rationale: Recurred in #163 (browsePractices returned ALL visible rows with ~3N+1 queries and no limit, unlike its bounded sibling surfacing endpoint).

title: When a gating flag flips off, clear the overrides it gated
rule: If a managers_can_* flag governs stored per-scope overrides, turning it off must delete those overrides in every storage shape (flat and structured) so a later re-enable cannot resurrect stale values.
rationale: Recurred in #107 (flat settings cleared gated rows on flag-off but structured anomaly_config rows were left and took effect again on re-enable).

title: Validate blank/whitespace consistently across all inputs
rule: If one input is rejected with a trim-based blank check, apply the same trim check to every semantically similar input (and to copied/reverted payloads), or document why one is treated as opaque.
rationale: Recurred in #153 (editContribution guarded body with body === '' while requireActor used .trim(), so whitespace-only bodies slipped into version rows).

title: Search/list primitives must default to published state
rule: A visibility/search primitive that filters on scope but not lifecycle state returns draft/unpublished/removed content; default to published with explicit opt-in to widen, or pin an all-states contract with a test and doc note.
rationale: Recurred in #155 (searchContributions/listVisibleForViewer applied no default state filter, so an org-scoped draft was discoverable by every viewer once wired to a route).

title: Deleting an interaction's effect re-exposes the browser default it was masking
rule: When you remove what a UI interaction DID, ask what the browser still does on that interaction by default, and whether the removed effect was the only thing hiding it. A default is masked while the element unmounts on the same gesture; once the element survives, that default becomes permanent state. Fix the newly-exposed default in the same change (preventDefault, or restore the state explicitly) rather than shipping the deletion alone — and pick an assertion the test environment can actually observe (jsdom implements no mousedown focus, so assert the event's defaultPrevented, not activeElement).
rationale: #265: removing backdrop-click dismissal left the dialog OPEN under the browser's default mousedown blur, so focus parked on <body> and every keystroke after a misplaced click vanished — the same silent-input-loss class the fix existed to prevent, one character at a time. Previously the dialog unmounted on that gesture and the unmount effect restored focus, so the default was invisible.

title: Derive structured tokens from the trusted stream, not raw HTML
rule: Extract semantic tokens (tags/metrics) from the parser's token stream or post-sanitize output and gate them through the canonical vocabulary; never regex-scrape attributes from pre-sanitize rendered HTML.
rationale: Recurred in #158 (tag extraction regex-scanned pre-sanitize HTML for data-metric, letting authored raw HTML mint arbitrary out-of-vocabulary tags).

title: Don't introduce a second vocabulary that is translated 1:1 and discarded
rule: Before adding an internal type for a seam, check what the consumer does with it. If the only consumer immediately maps it field-for-field into the shape you already ship, and no code reads the discriminant for anything except deciding which of two fields to copy, the type is a second vocabulary for one fact — and the adapter that translates it is pure overhead. A long docstring arguing why the flatter form would be worse is a strong smell that the flatter form is what the wire already is. Match the internal type to the contract it feeds and delete the adapter.
rationale: #270: GitFetchProgress shipped as `{phase:'listing',discovered} | {phase:'fetching',done,total}` with a 16-line defence of why a nullable-total pair would be worse — then applyFetchProgress translated it into exactly that nullable pair, which was also the wire shape and the only thing any consumer read.

title: Never clobber good data on a swallowed fetch failure, and surface it
rule: On a caught fetch failure, do not push default/zero values into an unconditional UPSERT (track per-source success flags and carry forward prior values via COALESCE/excluded columns), and push the error to the durable errors[]/run-status/doctor channel so a silent failure can't mimic a legitimate empty result.
rationale: Recurred in #123 (getPRReviews failures were swallowed and the PR upserted with changes_requested_count=0, regressing a real value of 2, with no log line distinguishing the permission failure from genuinely clean reviews).

title: Emit a conditional claim from the one site that knows it is true, not from each exception site
rule: When a message asserts something that only holds if a later step actually committed ('the cursor has advanced past these', 'these were onboarded'), do not format-and-push it early and then enumerate the paths that must retract or suppress it. Enumerating is how you get two of three paths and miss the third — and the third is usually the one nobody was thinking about (a container deleted mid-run, a guard that turns a write into a no-op while the transaction still commits). Thread the formatted line out and emit it from the single site whose execution IS the condition — typically inside the closure that performs the commit-gated write, below its own guards. That one placement covers every discard path structurally, and it removes the retraction code rather than adding to it.
rationale: #275: the drop advisory claims 'nothing re-asks them', which is only true if the window was recorded as covered. The first version gated on a completeness flag and retracted by prefix-scan in the rollback handler — covering the incomplete-provider and rollback paths but not a container whose owner was deleted mid-run, where isWritable makes the cursor advance a no-op while the transaction still commits. Emitting from inside the cursor-advance closure covered all three and deleted both the gate and the retraction loop.

title: FTS5 bm25 weights count UNINDEXED columns
rule: FTS5 bm25() positional weights map to columns in declared order including UNINDEXED columns, so prefix the weight vector with 0.0 for any UNINDEXED join key and design ranking tests to exercise all weight slots.
rationale: Recurred in #155 (bm25(tbl,10,4,2) put 10.0 on the UNINDEXED contribution_id and tags fell to the default 1.0; the test passed only by coincidence).

title: Gate the control AND the write on every non-ready state of the query that feeds it
rule: When a form's options load from a second query, gate on every non-ready state, not just isPending: a FAILED query settles to isPending === false with no data, so an isPending-only gate flips the control from a disabled 'Loading…' to an ENABLED list holding nothing but its placeholder — which reads as 'there are none' rather than 'this never loaded'. Resolve the state through one shared helper and say which state it is. Gate the SUBMIT too whenever the field's unloaded value is indistinguishable from a legitimate choice (e.g. '' meaning both 'roster not loaded' and 'deliberately none'), or the race writes the legitimate-looking value silently. Moving such a query from page-mount to dialog-mount opens exactly this window.
rationale: #236: migrating the admin forms into modals moved the developer-roster query from page-mount to dialog-mount, so the options now arrive while the admin is looking at the control. The gate covered isPending but not isError, and AdminUsers gated the select but not Save — on a cold cache, typing an email and hitting Create before the roster landed created a user with developer_id: null, and the link is create-time-only (the row renders developer_name as read-only text), so the account was stranded unlinked with no UI path to fix it.

title: Guard a caller-supplied callback where it is invoked, not at a subset of call sites
rule: When a caller-supplied callback (progress listener, hook, observer) is invoked from inside code whose try/catch decides DATA COMPLETENESS, a throw from that callback is indistinguishable from the real failure the catch exists for — so it can hold a cursor, drop a window, or discard a whole source. Put the try/catch at the single place the callback is actually invoked, so every emission site is covered including pre-existing ones; guarding a subset while the exported contract documents blanket coverage is worse than not guarding, because the sibling call sites are the ones nobody re-checks. Guard only the callback call, never the internal state mutation beside it — a throw there is your own bug and must stay loud. Then say plainly that a broken callback now fails silently, so its author knows to report its own errors.
rationale: #270: per-item progress reports moved INSIDE provider.getCommits/getPullRequests, whose per-repo catch reads a throw as a failed fetch — holding the provider's forward cursor and dropping its snapshots (#231). The first fix guarded 3 of 10 report sites while the exported listener doc claimed all of them; a listener throwing at any other site still got the whole provider skipped.

title: Hardening one fetch in a set that used to fail together breaks the coupling that made the others self-heal
rule: When several fetches in one run share a short failure budget, they fail TOGETHER — and a single incomplete one that holds the cursor causes every other failed window to be re-covered next run as a side effect. Lengthening the budget for one of them removes that free re-coverage: the hardened fetch heals, the run reports complete, the cursor advances, and a best-effort fetch that failed during the same outage is never retried because the next run's window starts above the advanced cursor (and per-item fan-outs are additionally gated by an updated-at window, so an item never touched again is never re-listed). Its fields are then frozen at a value that was never observed — which for a first sighting is zero. Either harden every member of the coupled set, or treat a retryable failure in the un-hardened ones as incomplete coverage so the window is honestly re-covered.
rationale: #272: the in-run repo retry initially covered only getCommits. getPullRequests and the per-PR getReviewComments/getPRReviews fan-out stayed on bare catch blocks that set an ok=false flag so the upsert 'carries forward' previous counts — which for a PR first seen during the outage is 0. Commits healing while the fan-out did not would have frozen review_comments_given/changes_requested/review_rounds permanently once the cursor moved past those PRs.

title: Memoizing a remote answer makes its wrong cases permanent and escapes the reset contract
rule: Before caching a remote response permanently, partition the responses into statements about the ENTITY (cacheable) and statements about the SERVER (never cacheable), and check the boundary cases: a 404 can mean 'no such sub-resource' or 'you may not see this', and a 200 can be silently truncated when a pagination header is stripped. Then ask what SELF-HEALING the memo removes — a failure path that re-covered the whole window used to re-ask, and now will not. Finally, add the table to every existing 'reset the data and resync' contract: a resync that reads a cache does not re-ask, so it converges on exactly the numbers the reset was run to discard.
rationale: #273: caching a per-commit diffstat is sound because it is immutable, but the 404-is-an-answer rule also freezes an access fault and a page-2 failure, and migrations 042/043 (the project's reset-and-resync remedy) do not clear the new table — so a reset would have replayed the poisoned rows byte-for-byte with no signal.

title: Evaluate merge conditions against the effective value, not the partial
rule: When merging a partial patch into stored config, any conditional cleanup must test the resolved/effective value, not the field present in the partial, or valid standalone edits get silently discarded.
rationale: Recurred in #107 (setMetricConfig dropped a just-set percentageBaseline because it checked merged.method, undefined in a baseline-only patch).

title: Nullable filter columns need T|null typing and IS NULL handling
rule: A filter over a nullable column must type the param as T|null and emit `col IS NULL` for the null case; `col = ?` bound to NULL is never true in SQL, so org-wide/null rows become unselectable.
rationale: Recurred in #151 (scopeTarget was typed string and bound scope_target = ?, so org rows with NULL could never be selected).

title: Compute period-attributed values as-of-period, not as-of-now
rule: When a value is attributed to a historical period, derive every label/tier/basis from data within that period's date range, not from the entity's full unbounded history as-of-now.
rationale: Recurred in #122 (the tier feeding basis/personal_insight scanned ALL snapshots ignoring asOf, relabeling a git-only May as 'measured' after Copilot connected in June).

title: Persist a floor/watermark that gates a disjoint additive backfill; never lazily default it from now
rule: When a stored floor/watermark bounds a disjoint additive backfill (the guard that keeps a re-fetch from overlapping already-imported data), record the TRUE floor at the moment its covered range is first established — the actual window start, or a real epoch sentinel for a walk-all — not a value re-derived from `now` at read time. A lazy `now − window` default is systematically too-recent (the real floor is `first_sync_time − window`), does not self-heal, and makes the FIRST backfill re-cover and additively double-count the overlap. Store an empty/walk-all boundary as a genuine sentinel timestamp so the truthiness check and the string-comparison guard both treat it correctly.
rationale: #229: getEarliestSyncedWatermark defaulted an un-backfilled provider's watermark to now−6mo, exact only for a UI 6-month first sync; a provider first-synced by the scheduled/CLI walk-all path has all history stored yet defaults too-recent, so its first 'sync older history' re-covered [now−12mo, now−6mo] and doubled commit counts. Fixed by recording the floor at first-sync time (epoch sentinel for walk-all).

title: Prove a gate-before-side-effect ordering with a load-bearing differential
rule: When code is deliberately ordered so a gate short-circuits BEFORE a privacy-relevant side effect (decrypt, produce plaintext, external call), the test must use an input that yields a DIFFERENT error if the side effect ran first (e.g. a forbidden request with a wrong key must return cloud_not_allowed, never decrypt_failed). A test that passes a valid input and asserts only the status code stays green even if the order is reversed.
rationale: #174: the cloud_not_allowed API test passed a VALID key and asserted only the 403, so a decrypt-then-gate reordering (which would produce plaintext for a denied request) would not have failed any test; fixed by a generator test using a wrong key as the differential.

title: Content edits must re-trigger timestamp-keyed approval gates
rule: When a publish gate authorizes based on an approval event after the last submit, editing content without emitting a new gating event allows submit→approve→edit→publish to ship unreviewed content; invalidate or re-submit approval on any edit-after-submit.
rationale: Recurred in #153 (editContribution appended a version but no review event, and the gate is timestamp-bound, not content-bound).

title: Scheme-allowlist any user-supplied URL rendered as a link, at both the write boundary and the renderer
rule: A user-supplied URL that will be rendered as an <a href> must be validated against an http(s) allowlist via new URL()+protocol at the write boundary (fail-closed), AND neutralized to plain text in the renderer when the scheme isn't http(s) — the two are separate trust boundaries (server and client can't share code), so a stored javascript:/data: link can't become a clickable stored-XSS vector through either path.
rationale: #189 (SEC-1): outcomeLink was rendered as <a href> with no scheme validation; added isValidOutcomeLink at the write boundary and safeHttpUrl neutralization in the renderer.

title: State keyed on reference identity needs a stable input
rule: When a hook or memo resets/derives state from a prop's REFERENCE identity (e.g. reset-page-1 on a new items array, or a useMemo keyed on columns), the caller must pass a STABLE reference — a list/array/object/columns built inline in the render body changes every render, so it resets forever or infinite-loops. The requirement is transitive: a table's post-sort rows identity depends on its columns reference, so an inline columns array resets a pageSize pager just as an inline rows array does. Use a module constant or useMemo, and document the stability contract (including transitive deps) on the hook/component.
rationale: #219: Leaderboard's inline `columns` array churned DataTable's sortedRows identity, snapping usePagination's pageSize pager back to page 1 on any parent re-render; separately, an inline `data ?? []` fallback each render would infinite-loop the identity-reset without a guard.

title: When you re-read stale state to fix an ordering bug, fix every consumer of it
rule: If a value is captured before a long-running or state-mutating step and later re-read inside the write boundary to fix a staleness bug, audit EVERY consumer of the original value in the same diff — fixing one consumer and leaving a sibling on the stale copy leaves the same bug with a smaller blast radius and no test covering it. Weight the audit by recoverability: a consumer whose input is re-delivered next run degrades, but one whose source is fetched by a moving watermark (PRs by updated_at) or discarded after the cursor advances loses the data permanently.
rationale: #256: the sync write path re-read buildDevLookupMap inside the transaction after auto-create so newly-minted developers' snapshots would project, but pr_records were still resolved against the pre-fetch map — so an auto-created developer's PRs that run were dropped, permanently, because providers re-fetch PRs by updated_at and a merged untouched PR is never re-delivered.

title: Widening a uniqueness key removes whatever the narrower key was silently collapsing
rule: Before widening a UNIQUE key to add an attribution column, enumerate the cases where the narrower key was COLLAPSING two writes into one row — that collapse may have been load-bearing de-duplication. Two scopes that legitimately overlap upstream (a group and its own subgroup, a parent and child path) can deliver the same underlying entity twice; under the narrow key the second write was an idempotent UPDATE, and under the wide key it becomes a second row that every downstream count now double-counts. Either reject the overlapping configuration at the boundary, or document it as unsupported AND detect it (doctor/create-time warning) rather than only noting it in a comment.
rationale: #264 widened `pr_records` from UNIQUE(provider, repo, pr_id) to UNIQUE(provider, container, repo, pr_id). GitLab providers append `include_subgroups=true`, so a provider for group `acme` and one for `acme/team1` list the same projects with the same path-with-namespace `repo` and the same `pr_id`. Pre-change the second was an UPDATE of the first (one row); after, it is two rows and `pr_review_metrics` counts the PR twice in prs_total/prs_merged/rework_rate.

title: Resolve sets in one query; no per-row fan-out or full scans
rule: Resolve cohort/membership/hidden-id sets once with a single JOIN/query before any loop and do in-memory checks inside, and fetch a single entity with a point-read plus the shared visibility check; never run O(N) per-row DB round-trips or scan the whole visible set and JS-filter to one row on every request.
rationale: Recurred in #132 (org opt-in resolution fired ~D×(3+2·prefs) synchronous queries), #161 (the pinned-practice loop re-ran the hides query per id), and #163 (loadVisiblePractice scanned all visible practices and .filter(...)[0] on every detail/history/feedback request).

title: Range-validate numeric/threshold config on both bounds
rule: Validators at a trust boundary must enforce upper bounds, integrality, and semantic ranges (not just finite-and-non-negative), and clamp privacy-protecting thresholds to a hard floor; checking only the lower bound lets an admin value exhaust resources or silently disable a safety guard.
rationale: Recurred in #107 (baselineWindow:100000000 the engine iterates per scan), #123 (rejectThreshold:50 / aiSignatureThreshold:0 made 'struggling' unreachable), and #159 (minSample:1 with no floor could expose one developer).

title: A field-mapping/DTO test must give each source field a distinct value
rule: When a test asserts that a normalized/DTO field is mapped from a specific source field, the fixture must give each candidate source field a DISTINCT value — if created_at, updated_at, merged_at all share one timestamp, a regression sourcing the target from the wrong field still passes the assertion. Pick values that differ so the assertion can only pass when the correct source field is read.
rationale: #247: the three provider PR-mapping tests asserted updatedAt inside a full-object toEqual, but every fixture set updated_at === created_at, so wiring updatedAt from created_at/merged_at would still have passed. Fixed by making each fixture's updated_* distinct from created_*.

title: A stricter guard needs the input class that only it handles
rule: When you replace a guard with a stricter or more total form — `=== undefined` to `Array.isArray`, a truthiness check to an explicit shape test, a two-state check to a three-state one — the existing fixtures were written for the looser form and almost never contain an input the two forms disagree on. So the added strictness ships with no test that can fail, and the next reviewer who calls it redundant is right on the evidence available. Add the input class that ONLY the new form handles (the non-array, the null, the NaN) and verify by experiment that reverting the guard fails exactly that test and nothing else. Do not let the justification live only in a comment: a comment cannot fail CI, and a comment that also overstates what the check inspects (a container test is not element validation) is worse than none.
rationale: #271: the sync loop's reuse guard was hardened from `rawCommit.diffs === undefined` to `Array.isArray(rawCommit.diffs)` so a non-array from a provider adapter would fall back rather than read as 'this commit touched nothing'. A reviewer verified that reverting it passed all 658 git tests — absent, `[]` and populated all behave identically under `!== undefined`, so the one branch the code argued hardest for was the one branch no fixture could distinguish.

title: An assertion that cannot fail independently of the layer that owns the behavior is not coverage
rule: Assert a shared primitive's behavior in the primitive's own suite, once. An assertion added at a wrapper or consumer layer that cannot diverge from the layer beneath it can only fail when that layer's tests are already red, so it adds lines and no detection — as does a composed test whose set-up step the component under test cannot observe. Before adding a case that restates an existing one, name the mutation it alone would catch; if there isn't one, either give it a unique failure mode (a different invariant reachable only from that composed state) or don't add it. Verify by re-introducing the bug and checking WHICH tests go red.
rationale: #265: one deleted onClick ended up asserted in 14 places. Mutation-testing the naive re-introduction turned 8 tests red — none of them in admin.test.tsx, whose 65 tests all passed with the regression present, because every surviving backdrop block sat inside a pending context where the guard blocks the close anyway. The new FormModal case could not diverge from Modal (FormModal renders no backdrop), and the new composed Escape case fired three events the handler-free backdrop cannot observe, hand-writing the state it claimed the click produced.

title: An emission no consumer can observe is not progress
rule: Before adding an emission — or restructuring control flow, or writing a test, to reach one — trace what the consumer actually reads. A reporter that overwrites a single latest-snapshot slot which a client polls means any emission followed synchronously (no await in between) by another is invisible: it is gone before the poll can sample it. So refactoring a labelled break into a flag purely to emit one final tick buys nothing, and a test pinning that tick is a change-detector on invisible behavior. The corollary matters more: an emission IS worth it exactly when a slow await follows it, which is why entering a step BEFORE its network request is the valuable placement and emitting after it is not.
rationale: #270: a labelled-break -> flag refactor in the Bitbucket commit walk existed to report the cutoff page's count, but the unconditional fan-out seed ran in the same synchronous block and always overwrote it. Compounding it, an earlier fix in the same branch removed the guard that had made that seed conditional — which is what made the tick unobservable, invalidating the round-1 rejection of the finding.

title: Enforce privacy structurally, not by a callsite allowlist
rule: When an aggregate object carries per-developer rows, don't spread it into responses behind a hand-maintained field allowlist; use a scope-pinned reader that cannot express the unsafe shape, plus an isAdmin backstop.
rationale: Recurred in #104 (privacy held only because the route copied eight scalars and dropped members) and #106 (manager routes relied solely on a middleware allowlist).

title: A call-to-action count must exclude rows the action should not be taken on
rule: When a panel, badge, or nudge derives a count from a list in order to urge an action, filter out the rows that list deliberately FLAGS but does not remove (likely-bot, archived, already-handled). A review surface and a call-to-action have opposite duties: the queue shows flagged rows so a human can override the classifier, while the CTA's count is the entire argument for acting — so an all-flagged list must produce no CTA at all, not a confident number pointing at rows nobody should promote.
rationale: #257: the cold-start onboarding panel counted `listAuthorCandidates` verbatim, which includes `likely_bot: true` rows because the classifier flags rather than filters. A repo whose only retained authors were dependabot[bot] and renovate rendered 'Sync retained commit history for 2 git authors — adding them attributes that retained history', steering an admin toward promoting two bots as developers.

title: A characterization test for a queued fix must pin the property, not the value the fix will change
rule: When you deliberately leave a known-wrong behavior in place and file a follow-up issue, the test that stops it changing SILENTLY must assert the property you actually want preserved — not the wrong value itself. Freezing the value makes the test a change-detector standing in the way of the queued fix, so whoever lands that fix must edit a test whose comment says it exists to protect the behavior. Assert the shape and the fact that the code path still runs (a call count, a phase tag); leave the number the fix will correct unpinned.
rationale: #270: a Bitbucket backfill walk that retains nothing reports a stationary 0, filed as a follow-up. The test asserted the exact array including `done: 0` — the very value the queued fix changes — while its comment claimed it existed to catch the pages no longer being reported at all.

title: A cleanup driven off a deferred-write set skips the failure paths that create the most to clean
rule: When a run collects a set inside its write transaction (which containers were orphaned, which rows were skipped) and then reuses that set to drive a cleanup, check which paths populate NONE of the closures that fill it. A rolled-back transaction that deliberately clears the set, a fetch that threw before any closure was pushed, and a mode that skips the accounting entirely (a backfill with no cursor advance and no stall update) are all reachable — and they are precisely the failing runs that left the most behind. Drive the cleanup off the run's OWN input set instead, and keep the reporting set separate: the report describes discarded writes, the cleanup describes rows to retract, and a rolled-back run has the second without the first.
rationale: #273: the mid-run purge of a deleted container's cache rows was driven off `orphanedContainers`, which only the write transaction's closures populate — so it was skipped on rollback, on a thrown fetch, and on a failed backfill, i.e. exactly the runs whose partial rows the feature exists to preserve.

title: A degradation counter must count only what its signal claims to describe
rule: When a swallowed-error counter drives an operator-visible signal, count ONLY the conditions that signal names. Folding in a deterministic per-item refusal — a correct, permanent decision about one record's data — makes the signal fire on every run forever on a healthy system, which trains the operator to skim past the one line that is supposed to mean the feature is dead. Check the units too: a counter incremented once per batch and once per item in the same field understates a batch failure by orders of magnitude, and the message must describe what actually happened for each kind (a failed READ did not lose the writes).
rationale: #273: the diffstat cache's fault counter incremented both for a database error and for refusing a value its reader would reject. One un-nameable file entry anywhere in a repo's history would have made 'Diffstat cache degraded' fire on every scheduled sync forever — the exact signal dilution the advisory was added to prevent.

title: A new operator signal must supplement the old one, and name its scope
rule: When adding a finer-grained progress/health indicator, do not substitute it for the coarse one it improves on: check how much of the run the new signal is present for (often nearly all of it), because that is how much of the time the old signal becomes unrenderable. The coarse counter usually answers a different question — how much work the run has actually banked — and losing it is a regression the acceptance criteria never asked for. When both are shown, LABEL the scopes: two counters using the same noun where the finer one is routinely the LARGER (a within-item position vs. a completed-item total) reads as one broken number. Also check what else keyed off the old signal's low volatility — a live region that was tolerable only because the string rarely changed becomes a once-per-poll announcement.
rationale: #270: the within-repo counter first replaced `N commits · M PRs`, which is non-null for nearly the whole fetching stage, so the run-level totals became visible only under backend/bundle skew. Restoring them exposed two more problems: `commit 1240/5000 · 34 commits` reads as a bug (the within-repo count is normally larger), and the now-volatile string sat in a `role="status"` live region that would announce it every second for a multi-hour sync.

title: A partial-update endpoint must not treat an omitted field as a destructive reset
rule: A PATCH/update that always rewrites every column from the parsed body turns an omitted optional field into a silent reset (e.g. omitting repos re-enables monitor-all). Make the server only touch fields actually present in the body, or require an explicit clear sentinel (repos: null); do not rely on the UI re-sending stored values to prevent a destructive default.
rationale: #192: updateProvider always rewrote repos_include/repos_exclude, so an omitted repos widened scope to every repo in the org; only client-side preserve-helpers stood between a second consumer (script/curl) and a silent scope blow-out.

title: A reuse/cache field must distinguish 'not supplied' from 'supplied and empty'
rule: When an optional field carries a value fetched upstream so a downstream consumer can skip re-fetching it, the absent state and the empty state are DIFFERENT answers and must stay distinguishable: `undefined` means 'nobody supplied this, go get it', `[]`/`0`/`''` means 'already obtained, and it is empty'. Branch on presence or shape (`Array.isArray`, `in`), never on truthiness — collapsing the two sends exactly the empty cases back down the path the field exists to avoid, and those are often the cases that were empty because the remote endpoint already refused them (a 404 swallowed into an empty result), so the retry is guaranteed to fail again. Every producer must then set the field unconditionally, including on its own error/degradation branches, and the contract must say which.
